facts.statement: Grippia is a genus containing only one known species, Grippia longirostris.
facts.quote: Its only species is Grippia longirostris.

facts.statement: Grippia longirostris was a small ichthyopterygian measuring approximately 1 to 1.5 meters in length.
facts.quote: It was a relatively small ichthyopterygian, measuring around 1 – 1.5 m long.

facts.statement: Members of Grippia longirostris swam using lateral tail movements similar to those of a modern-day eel.
facts.quote: Members of this species swam via lateral movements of their tail similar to that of a modern-day eel.

facts.statement: No skull of Grippia has been found with a snout, making all descriptions of this feature speculative.
facts.quote: An important thing to note is how no skull has been found to have a snout; therefore any descriptions of the snout are speculative.

facts.statement: The most recent detailed descriptions of Grippia's forelimbs were performed in 1998 by Ryosuke Motani.
facts.quote: The most recent descriptions of the forelimbs were performed in 1998 by Motani.

facts.statement: Studies of Grippia's forelimbs revealed that the species possessed pentadactyl limbs.
facts.quote: This study revealed: Grippia possesses pentadactyl limbs.

facts.statement: Grippia is believed to have lived between 250 and 235 million years ago during the Olenekian to Anisian stages of the Early to Mid-Triassic.
facts.quote: Grippia are believed to have lived from 250 to 235 Ma during the Olenekian – Anisian of the early to mid-Triassic.

facts.statement: Grippia inhabited shallow coastal seas located at equatorial latitudes.
facts.quote: It inhabited equatorial to equatorial shallow coastal seas.

facts.statement: Analysis of dental remains suggests Grippia practiced an omnivorous feeding style, though this is debated due to the lack of a complete skull.
facts.quote: Analysis of dental remains belonging to G. longirostris has shown blunt posterior teeth and replacement maxillary teeth, which suggests that it practiced an omnivorous feeding style.

facts.statement: It is debated what Grippia ate because existing fossil samples lack a snout, making dietary conclusions highly speculative.
facts.quote: All of these results were based on samples that did not include an existing snout, therefore they were highly speculative and paleontologists will not know what Grippia ate until a full skull is found.

facts.statement: Grippia is estimated to have gone extinct around 235 million years ago.
facts.quote: This limited the amount of food that Grippia could secure, eventually leading it to its extinction around 235 Ma.

facts.statement: The first skull of Grippia longirostris was discovered in 1929.
facts.quote: The first G. longirostris skull was found in 1929.

facts.statement: The first and fifth metacarpals and phalanges of Grippia are lunate in appearance and concave inward toward the interior carpals.
facts.quote: The first and fifth metacarpals and phalanges are lunate in appearance and concave inwards towards the interior carpals.

facts.statement: In Grippia skulls, the quadratojugal bone does not enter the upper temporal fenestra.
facts.quote: The quadratojugal does not enter the upper temporal fenestra.

facts.statement: The anterior margin of the external naris in Grippia is formed by the premaxilla bone.
facts.quote: The anterior margin of the external naris is formed by the premaxilla.
